source.title: How many degrees of freedom do we need to train deep networks: a loss landscape perspective
source.authors: Brett W. Larsen; Stanislav Fort; Nico Becker; S. Ganguli

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the full paper and supplement.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains models in random and burn-in affine subspaces and measures training accuracy, testing training success as a function of trainable dimension rather than testing the claim's usual full-parameter training recipe.
record.gate_note: The study reports training-accuracy phase transitions and burn-in comparisons. It also reports test-accuracy results, but those do not measure the training error named in V1. Figures provide the accuracy curves; the text does not give exact training-accuracy values for individual conditions. Lottery-ticket comparisons are described but are not included as rows because they are not the claim's training method.
record.test_reason: The study measures training classification accuracy of convolutional networks trained with Adam on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, using restricted affine subspaces. These results bear on V1, but the supplied text does not reveal whether training error approaches zero. A phase transition in reaching a chosen accuracy does not itself establish near-zero error.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. More precisely, the authors connect successful low-dimensional training to a large local angular dimension of the target loss sublevel set around initialization, explain the general burn-in advantage geometrically, and compare random subspaces with pruning and lottery subspaces. They do not conclude that these experiments establish near-zero training error.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Adam optimization in restricted random or burn-in affine subspaces, rather than ordinary full-parameter gradient training; full-model runs are same-epoch baselines. The initialization and optimization recipe details are in the appendix.
record.method_sensitivity: Threshold training dimension varies with desired accuracy, initialization quality/burn-in time, and architecture/dataset; more burn-in lowers the threshold for some desired accuracies. Number of runs and δ differ by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Success at a chosen accuracy undergoes a sharp transition as random-subspace dimension increases; higher target accuracy generally requires more dimensions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Restricted random-subspace training exhibits an accuracy-dependent threshold training dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: Burn-in generally reduces the dimensions needed to reach selected accuracies. Appendix A.3 reports no apparent burn-in advantage for Conv-3 on MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brief unrestricted pretraining can reduce the subsequent random-subspace dimension needed for a target accuracy, with architecture and dataset exceptions.

record.problems: Training accuracies and curve-specific threshold values are conveyed in figures without numerical transcription in the supplied text. Training used few epochs, with 10, 5, or 3 runs depending on the experiment; the authors adjusted δ for the smaller run counts. The measured success probability is an approximation because Adam may not find the minimum loss in a subspace.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Test-accuracy curves are outside the training-error claim. Lottery-ticket and lottery-subspace comparisons are not rows for this claim's training recipe.

untested.parts: Corrupted or random labels; systematic model-size, regularization, or stopping-time comparisons; eventual convergence under ordinary unrestricted training. Near-zero error cannot be assessed from the supplied figure text.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and the effect of one or two additional student neurons.
Training degradation with depth and controlled comparisons with identity shortcuts.
Activation-matched initialization, signal or gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth. Burn-in is a different initialization intervention.
Learning rates relative to a measured stability threshold, curvature trajectories, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Controlled normalization comparisons and Fixup. Using batch normalization in ResNet20 does not test its training advantage.

missing.what: Readable CIFAR training-accuracy endpoints and full-model baseline accuracies are needed to determine whether V1's near-zero-error effect occurs. The record describes these baselines but records no accuracy values.
missing.locator: Figures 2, 3, 7 and 8; horizontal full-model baseline lines

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V1 labels: unspecified high accuracy does not establish near-zero error, and a burn-in advantage alone is not a scope limitation of V1. Figure ordinates are unavailable in the supplied text. The measured success probabilities approximate geometric intersection probabilities because Adam may fail to find an available solution.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test corrupted or random labels, regularized recipes, smaller models, or early stopping as a cause of substantial training error. It tests random affine-subspace training and burn-in variants, not ordinary full-parameter training alone.
